## TL;DR

Engineer turns already ran in their own process group, but an agent CLI's own
shell tool can start a test runner in a new session (`setsid`, `detached`) or
leave it reparented to PID 1. Those children were invisible to the group reap
and to the test-helper sweeper, which only knew about `repoos-vitest-*` temp
roots. Seven orphaned `vitest` processes then pinned a laptop for an hour.

This change adds two layers. Turn teardown now collects the turn's PID tree,
processes whose cwd is inside the turn's worktree, and processes carrying a new
`REPOOS_TURN_MARKER` env value, then sends TERM to exact PIDs and KILL after a
grace period, re-scanning once in case something daemonized meanwhile. A
control-plane sweeper runs every 15 seconds, finds reparented same-uid
processes in managed worktrees or carrying this checkout's marker that no live
turn owns, stops them by exact PID, and records each kill with task id,
command, CPU time and age in the system log, the task activity log, the
dashboard, the pressure guard and the CTO digest. The test-helper
`sweepOrphanedRunRootProcesses` is now wall-clock and size bounded.

## Work and rationale

The new `src/core/run-processes.ts` is the shared primitive. It parses one
`ps axo pid,ppid,pgid,uid,etime,time,%cpu,command` sweep, builds parent-link
trees, reads process cwds in one batch (`/proc/<pid>/cwd` on Linux, one `lsof`
on macOS), and reads `REPOOS_TURN_MARKER` from `/proc/<pid>/environ` where the
OS exposes it. Matching is deliberately structural: PID tree membership,
path-boundary-safe worktree cwd, or an exact marker minted by this checkout.
There is no name matching anywhere, and every kill targets one numeric PID.

Two classifiers keep the sweeper and teardown honest. `findOrphanedRunProcesses`
requires the same uid, `ppid === 1`, a minimum age, a managed-worktree cwd or a
repo-scoped marker, and no live turn (PID tree, workdir or marker). It returns
the original `ps` facts plus the worktree and task id. `findEscapedTurnProcesses`
is the teardown view: it includes tree descendants even when they left the group,
plus cwd and marker matches. A cwd-only match must have started during the turn,
so an older human dev server in the same worktree is not collateral damage.

`reapAgentTurnProcessTree` signals the turn's group and the escaped PIDs with
TERM, waits, re-scans (a child may have daemonized during the grace), then
signals KILL to survivors and returns what was found, what got KILL, and what
survived. `AgentRunner.finalizeTurn` awaits it instead of the old synchronous
group reap and writes a transcript note naming any escaped PIDs it stopped.
Agent spawns now carry a repo-scoped `REPOOS_TURN_MARKER`; `AgentRunner.running()`
also exposes `runId` and `turnMarker` so the sweeper can spare live turns.

`src/server/run-process-reaper.ts` wraps that for the control plane. It maps
live turns from the runner, derives the task id from branch-shaped worktree
paths (or the marker), kills what is left, logs each kill through
`logger.system`, calls back into `AgentRunner.recordActivity`, and keeps the
last sweep for the dashboard and CTO. The server arms it five seconds after
boot and every fifteen seconds on the control plane only (preview children and
port-0 test servers never sweep). The pressure guard gained
`OrphanedRunPressureInfo`: still-running orphans are a critical reason with
PIDs, already-reaped ones are advisory, and a provider lets queue starts and
gate waits see the same census. `sampleSystem` passes the reaper's findings into
`SystemStats.runProcesses`; the System Resources panel shows task id, PID,
command, CPU time and age, and the CTO digest gets its own "Orphaned run
processes" section that also feeds the material-change hash.

`collectOrphanedRunRoots` bounds the test-helper sweep: a deadline (default
5s), row and root caps, a skip for agent-prompt-sized command lines, and a
larger `ps` buffer. It warns when it truncates instead of walking forever.

## Approaches tried

The first cut relied only on the PID tree, snapshotting descendants before the
group kill. That misses a grandchild whose parent already exited and
reparented to PID 1, so cwd and the inherited marker became necessary. A
marker-only design was rejected: on macOS SIP hides another process's
environment, so cwd and the tree have to carry macOS.

The first integrated live test compared `lsof`'s cwd to the fixture path
directly and failed on macOS because `/tmp` resolves to `/private/tmp`. Path
comparison now resolves symlinks best-effort in `pathInside`, with the plain
absolute path as fallback.

The first remote run exposed a test that assumed cwd matching; on Linux the
grandchild inherited the marker, so the classifier correctly reported
`run-marker` first. The cwd test now deliberately withholds the marker from the
grandchild, keeping both paths covered.

The remote validation host was under heavy load on repeated runs: timeouts in
`debugger-integration`, `agent-review` and `remote-host-pool` (all spawn-heavy,
none touched by this diff) came and went, while those files pass in isolation
here. Running the full changed suite locally under Bun with a stable `TMPDIR`
passed all 439 files. Without that stable `TMPDIR`, two local attempts failed
for an unrelated reason: RepoOS restarted the agent turn mid-check and removed
its `agent-run-tmp` directory, so Vite's cache and the UI smoke's `mkdtemp`
disappeared underneath the still-running check. That is the same
turn-outlives-its-process bug from this task, seen from the other side, and it
is why the handoff gate, not a long-lived shell command, is the authoritative
run. I also stopped two vitest workers left orphaned for three and four days in
old task worktrees — exact PIDs saved from `ps`, no name matching — which freed
CPU for the final local gate.

## Challenges and blockers

No human blocker. The main design risk was collateral damage: a cwd-wide scan
could stop a human's long-lived server in a task worktree. The turn-start age
gate and the live-workdir/live-tree exclusions make the sweep conservative.
The other risk was cost: early versions ran `lsof` against every process.
Candidates are now narrowed to reparented processes (the only ones that can
have escaped) before the cwd probe, and the sweeper only scans on the control
plane.

macOS's inability to read another process's environment is documented rather
than worked around with privileged probes. Linux gets both signals; macOS gets
the tree and cwd, which the live test proves on this machine.

## Key learnings

A process group is a lifecycle hint, not a boundary: any tool that can call
`setsid` escapes it, and once the parent exits the PID tree is gone too. Durable
handles have to be things the process carries with it — its cwd and its
environment. Those handles need repo scoping so one checkout's sweeper never
kills another checkout's live run. Symlink-normalised path comparison matters
more than expected on macOS. And the bounded sweep is not cosmetic: one
pathological `ps` command line was enough to hang `beforeAll` before, which is
why the new scan has an explicit deadline and caps.
